questions.q: For a qubit state |ψ⟩ = a|0⟩ + b|1⟩, what does the Born rule say?
options: P(0) = a and P(1) = b, directly
P(0) = |a|² and P(1) = |b|²
P(0) = a + b and P(1) = a − b
P(0) and P(1) are always exactly 0.5 regardless of a and b
questions.explain: The Born rule converts amplitudes into probabilities by squaring their magnitude: P(0) = |a|², P(1) = |b|². This is why amplitudes can be negative or complex while probabilities are always non-negative real numbers.

questions.q: For the state 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩, what are P(0) and P(1), and how do you know this state is validly normalized?
options: P(0)=0.6, P(1)=0.8; normalized because 0.6+0.8=1.4
P(0)=0.48, P(1)=0.48; normalized because they're equal
questions.explain: Squaring each amplitude: 0.6²=0.36 and 0.8²=0.64. Checking normalization means these probabilities must sum to 1, and 0.36+0.64=1.00 confirms the state is validly normalized.

questions.q: Measuring |+⟩ = (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 in the computational basis gives P(0)=P(1)=0.5. What does this reveal about measurement statistics in general?
options: That any two states giving the same measurement statistics in one basis must be identical states
That measurement statistics in a single basis don't always fully distinguish states — |−⟩ gives the identical 0.5/0.5 split in this basis despite being a clearly different state from |+⟩
That |+⟩ cannot be a valid normalized state because the probabilities are equal
That a 50/50 split means the qubit was never actually in superposition
questions.explain: |+⟩ and |−⟩ have different amplitudes (relative sign) and behave completely differently under the Hadamard gate, yet both give exactly 50/50 computational-basis measurement statistics. This shows that measurement in one basis alone doesn't always reveal everything about a state.

questions.q: When you run a quantum circuit on real hardware and read out the result, what do you actually get back?
options: The complete vector of amplitudes for every possible outcome
A printout of each qubit's exact quantum state before measurement
Exactly one classical bitstring, sampled probabilistically according to the Born rule — you must repeat many runs to estimate the underlying probabilities
A guaranteed deterministic bitstring that is always the same for a given circuit
questions.explain: Hardware never hands back the amplitude vector directly. Each run yields one classical sample drawn according to the Born-rule probabilities; recovering the probability distribution requires repeating the circuit many times and tallying outcomes.

questions.q: Why must quantum algorithms be specifically designed so the correct answer has high measurement probability?
options: Because the Born rule means you only get a probabilistic classical sample at the end, so unless interference has concentrated probability on the right answer, you'll rarely sample it even if the circuit's intermediate math was elegant
Because quantum computers always return the amplitude with the largest numeric value regardless of probability
Because the Born rule guarantees the correct answer automatically has the highest probability in any circuit
Because measurement doesn't actually involve probability once a circuit is complete
questions.explain: Since readout gives only a probabilistic one-shot sample, algorithm design must use interference to push the correct answer's probability close to 1 and wrong answers' probabilities close to 0 — otherwise you'd sample the right answer only rarely, however elegant the circuit's structure.
